title: Complement of Reflexive Relation
theorem_text:
Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation.
Then $\RR$ is reflexive if and only if its complement $\relcomp {S \times S} \RR \subseteq S \times S$ is antireflexive.
Likewise, $\RR$ is antireflexive if and only if its complement $\relcomp {S \times S} \RR \subseteq S \times S$ is reflexive.
proof_text:
Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be reflexive.
Then:
$\forall x \in S: \tuple {x, x} \in \RR$
By the definition of complement of $\RR$:
$\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \implies \tuple {x, y} \notin \relcomp {S \times S} \RR$
The same applies to $\tuple {x, x}$, and thus:
$\forall x \in S: \tuple {x, x} \notin \relcomp {S \times S} \RR$
Thus $\relcomp {S \times S} \RR$ is antireflexive.
Similarly, by definition:
$\forall x \in S: \tuple {x, x} \notin \RR \implies \neg \tuple {x, x} \notin \relcomp {S \times S} \RR$
By Double Negation it follows that:
$\tuple {x, x} \in \relcomp {S \times S} \RR$
The converses of these results follow from the fact that:
$\relcomp {S \times S} {\relcomp {S \times S} \RR} = \RR$
by Relative Complement of Relative Complement.
review_reason: Taking the complement in the square switches membership of each diagonal pair. Complementing twice returns the original relation and supplies both converses.

title: Epimorphism Preserves Commutativity
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ and $\left({T, *}\right)$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: \left({S, \circ}\right) \to \left({T, *}\right)$ be an epimorphism.
Let $\circ$ be a commutative operation.
Then $*$ is also a commutative operation.
proof_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be an algebraic structure in which $\circ$ is commutative.
Let $\phi: \left({S, \circ}\right) \to \left({T, *}\right)$ be an epimorphism.
As an epimorphism is surjective, it follows that:
$\forall u, v \in T: \exists x, y \in S: \phi \left({x}\right) = u, \phi \left({y}\right) = v$
So:
$$u * v = \phi \left({x}\right) * \phi \left({y}\right)$$
$\phi$ is a surjection
$$= \phi \left({x \circ y}\right)$$
Morphism Property
$$= \phi \left({y \circ x}\right)$$
Commutativity of $\circ$
$$= \phi \left({y}\right) * \phi {\left({x}\right)}$$
Morphism Property
$$= v * u$$
by definition as above
review_reason: Surjectivity supplies preimages for both target elements. Commuting the two source factors and applying the homomorphism property reverses the target factors.

title: Epimorphism Preserves Identity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be an epimorphism.
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ have an identity element $e_S$.
Then $\struct {T, *}$ has the identity element $\map \phi {e_S}$.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure in which $\circ$ has an identity $e_S$.
Then:
$\forall x \in S: x \circ e_S = x = e_S \circ x$
Thus:
$$\map \phi x = \map \phi {x \circ e_S}$$
$e_S$ is an identity for $\circ$
$$= \map \phi x * \map \phi {e_S}$$
Morphism property of $\circ$ under $\phi$
and:
$$\map \phi x = \map \phi {e_S \circ x}$$
$e_S$ is an identity for $\circ$
$$= \map \phi {e_S} * \map \phi x$$
Morphism property of $\circ$ under $\phi$
The result follows because every element $y \in T$ is of the form $\map \phi x$ with $x \in S$.
review_reason: The image of the source identity fixes each image element on both sides. Surjectivity extends this check to all of T.

title: Epimorphism Preserves Inverses
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ and $\left({T, *}\right)$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: \left({S, \circ}\right) \to \left({T, *}\right)$ be an epimorphism.
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ have an identity $e_S$.
Let $x^{-1}$ be an inverse element of $x$ for $\circ$.
Then $\phi \left({x^{-1}}\right)$ is an inverse element of $\phi \left({x}\right)$ for $*$.
That is:
$\phi \left({x^{-1}}\right) = \left({\phi \left({x}\right)}\right)^{-1}$
proof_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be an algebraic structure in which $\circ$ has an identity element $e_S$.
From Epimorphism Preserves Identity, it follows that $\left({T, *}\right)$ also has an identity element, which is $\phi \left({e_S}\right)$.
Let $y$ be an inverse of $x$ in $\left({S, \circ}\right)$.
Then:
$$\phi \left({x}\right) * \phi \left({y}\right) = \phi \left({x \circ y}\right)$$
$$= \phi \left({e_S}\right)$$
$$= \phi \left({y \circ x}\right)$$
$$= \phi \left({y}\right) * \phi \left({x}\right)$$
So $\phi \left({y}\right)$ is an inverse of $\phi \left({x}\right)$ in $\left({T, *}\right)$.
review_reason: Applying the homomorphism to both inverse identities gives the identity of T on both sides, because surjectivity ensures the identities correspond.

title: Homomorphism with Cancellable Codomain Preserves Identity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct{S, \circ}$ and $\struct{T, *}$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: \struct{S, \circ} \to \struct{T, *}$ be a homomorphism.
Let $\struct{S, \circ}$ have an identity $e_S$.
Let $\struct{T, *}$ have an identity $e_T$.
Let every element of $\struct{T, *}$ be cancellable.
Then $\map \phi {e_S}$ is the identity $e_T$.
proof_text:
Let $\struct{S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure in which $\circ$ has an identity $e_S$.
Let $\struct{T, *}$ be an algebraic structure in which $*$ has an identity $e_T$.
Let $\struct{T, *}$ be such that every element is cancellable.
Let $\phi: \struct{S, \circ} \to \struct{T, *}$ be a homomorphism.
Every element of $\struct{T, *}$ is cancellable.
Suppose there is an idempotent element in $\struct{T, *}$
So from Identity is only Idempotent Cancellable Element, it must be the identity $e_T$.
Thus:
$$\map \phi {e_S} * \map \phi {e_S} = \map \phi {e_S \circ e_S}$$
by the morphism property of $\circ$ under $\phi$
$$= \map \phi {e_S}$$
as $e_S$ is the identity of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$
So $\map \phi {e_S}$ is idempotent in $\struct{T, *}$ and the result follows.
review_reason: The image of the identity is idempotent. Cancellation in the target then forces this element to equal its identity.

title: Homomorphism with Identity Preserves Inverses
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ and $\left({T, *}\right)$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: \left({S, \circ}\right) \to \left({T, *}\right)$ be a homomorphism.
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ have an identity $e_S$.
Let $\left({T, *}\right)$ also have an identity $e_T = \phi \left({e_S}\right)$.
If $x^{-1}$ is an inverse of $x$ for $\circ$, then $\phi \left({x^{-1}}\right)$ is an inverse of $\phi \left({x}\right)$ for $*$.
That is:
$\phi \left({x^{-1}}\right) = \left({\phi \left({x}\right)}\right)^{-1}$
proof_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be an algebraic structure in which $\circ$ has an identity $e_S$.
Let $\phi: \left({S, \circ}\right) \to \left({T, *}\right)$ be a homomorphism.
Let $\left({T, *}\right)$ be an algebraic structure in which $*$ has an identity $e_T = \phi \left({e_S}\right)$.
$$\phi \left({x}\right) * \phi \left({x^{-1} }\right) = \phi \left({x \circ x^{-1} }\right)$$
Morphism property of $\phi$
$$= \phi \left({e_S}\right) = e_T$$
$$= \phi \left({x^{-1} \circ x}\right)$$
$$= \phi \left({x^{-1} }\right) * \phi \left({x}\right)$$
Morphism property of $\phi$
review_reason: Both orders of the product of the two images equal the image of the source identity, which by hypothesis is the target identity.

title: Homomorphism to Group Preserves Identity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure.
Let $\struct {T, *}$ be a group.
Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be a homomorphism.
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ have an identity $e_S$.
Then:
$\map \phi {e_S} = e_T$
proof_text:
By hypothesis, $\struct {T, *}$ is a group.
By the Cancellation Laws, all elements of $T$ are cancellable.
Thus Homomorphism with Cancellable Codomain Preserves Identity can be applied.
review_reason: The group codomain is cancellative and has an identity, so the cited identity-preservation result applies.

title: Monomorphism Image is Isomorphic to Domain
theorem_text:
The image of a monomorphism is isomorphic to its domain.
That is, if $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ is a monomorphism, then:
$\phi: S_1 \to \Img \phi$
is an isomorphism.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {S_1, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \circ_2}$ be closed algebraic structures.
Let $\phi$ be a monomorphism from $\struct {S_1, \circ_1}$ to $\struct {S_2, \circ_2}$.
Let $T = \Img \phi$ be the image of $\phi$.
By Morphism Property Preserves Closure, $\struct {T, \circ_2}$ is closed.
As $\phi$ is a monomorphism, it is by definition an injective homomorphism.
From Restriction of Injection is Injection, $\phi: S_1 \to \Img \phi$ is an injection.
From Restriction of Mapping to Image is Surjection, $\phi: S_1 \to \Img \phi$ is a surjection.
Thus $\phi \to \Img \phi$ is by definition a bijection.
Thus $\phi: S_1 \to \Img \phi$ is a bijective homomorphism.
Hence, by definition, $\phi: S_1 \to \Img \phi$ is an isomorphism.
review_reason: Restriction of the codomain to the closed image preserves injectivity and makes the homomorphism onto, giving the required isomorphism.

title: Inverse Mapping in Induced Structure
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be an algebraic structure.
Let $\left({T, \oplus}\right)$ be an abelian group.
Let $f$ be a homomorphism from $S$ into $T$.
Let $f^*$ be the induced structure inverse of $f$.
Then $f^*$ is a homomorphism from $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ into $\left({T, \oplus}\right)$.
proof_text:
Let $\left({T, \oplus}\right)$ be an abelian group.
Let $x, y \in S$.
Then:
$$f^* \left({x \circ y}\right) = \left({f \left({x \circ y}\right)}\right)^{-1}$$
Induced Structure Inverse
$$= \left({f \left({x}\right) \oplus f \left({y}\right)}\right)^{-1}$$
$f$ is a homomorphism
$$= \left({f \left({y}\right) \oplus f \left({x}\right)}\right)^{-1}$$
Commutativity of $\oplus$
$$= \left({f \left({x}\right)}\right)^{-1} \oplus \left({f \left({y}\right)}\right)^{-1}$$
Inverse of Group Product
$$= f^* \left({x}\right) \oplus f^* \left({y}\right)$$
Induced Structure Inverse
review_reason: The abelian target allows the factors to be swapped before taking the inverse of the product. The resulting factors are exactly the pointwise inverses in the required order.

title: Inverse Completion of Commutative Semigroup is Inverse Completion of Itself
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a commutative semigroup.
Let $\left ({C, \circ}\right) \subseteq \left({S, \circ}\right)$ be the subsemigroup of cancellable elements of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$.
Let $\left({T, \circ'}\right)$ be an inverse completion of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$.
Then $\left({T, \circ'}\right)$ is its own inverse completion.
proof_text:
Let $x \circ' y^{-1}$ be cancellable for $\circ'$, where $x \in S$ and $y \in C$.
We have that $y$ is invertible for $\circ'$.
So by Invertible Element of Associative Structure is Cancellable:
$y$ is cancellable for $\circ'$.
Now by definition of inverse element:
$x = \left({x \circ' y^{-1}}\right) \circ' y$
Thus $x$ is also cancellable for $\circ'$.
By Cancellable Elements of Semigroup form Subsemigroup, $x$ is cancellable for $\circ$.
So:
$x \in S \implies x \in C$
Thus $x$ is invertible for $\circ'$.
Hence by Inverse of Product in Associative Structure:
$x \circ' y$ is invertible for $\circ'$.
So every cancellable element of $\left({T, \circ'}\right)$ is invertible.
So, by definition, $\left({T, \circ'}\right)$ is its own inverse completion.
review_reason: Multiplication by the unit y shows x is cancellable in the completion and hence on its subsemigroup S. Therefore x and y are units in the completion, so the original fraction is a unit too; the last display mentions xy, but the same unit-product rule immediately covers xy-inverse.

title: Identity of Inverse Completion of Commutative Monoid
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a commutative monoid whose identity is $e$.
Let $\left ({C, \circ}\right) \subseteq \left({S, \circ}\right)$ be the subsemigroup of cancellable elements of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$.
Let $\left({T, \circ'}\right)$ be an inverse completion of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$.
Then $e \in T$ is the identity for $\circ'$.
proof_text:
Let $e$ be the identity for $\circ$.
Let $e = x \circ' y^{-1}$, where $x \in S, y \in C$.
Then:
$$y = e \circ y$$
Definition of Identity
$$= \left({x \circ' y^{-1} }\right) \circ' y$$
Definition of Inverse
$$= x \circ' \left({y^{-1} \circ' y}\right)$$
$\circ'$ is associative
$$= x \circ' e$$
Definition of Inverse
Thus $e = y^{-1} \circ' y$, and $y^{-1} \circ' y$ is the identity for $\circ'$.
review_reason: Substituting the source identity e for the product of y-inverse and y already assumes e is the identity of the completion, precisely what must be proved.

title: Inverse Completion Theorem
theorem_text: Every commutative semigroup containing cancellable elements admits an inverse completion.
proof_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a commutative semigroup which has cancellable elements.
From Construction of Inverse Completion, we can construct an inverse completion $\left({T', \oplus'}\right)$ of $\left({S', \oplus'}\right)$, which is an isomorphic copy of $S$ under the mapping $\psi: S \to S'$.
By the Embedding Theorem, there exists a semigroup $\left({T, \circ}\right)$  which contains $\left({S, \circ}\right)$, and an isomorphism $\Psi$ from $\left({T, \circ}\right)$ to $\left({T', \oplus'}\right)$ which extends $\psi$.
Thus $T$ is an inverse completion of $S$.
review_reason: The construction supplies a completion for an isomorphic copy of S, and the embedding theorem transports that entire structure back along an isomorphism extending the identification of S.

title: Extension Theorem for Isomorphisms
theorem_text:
Let the following conditions be fulfilled:
: Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a commutative semigroup with cancellable elements
: Let $\phi$ be an isomorphism from $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ into a semigroup $\left({T, *}\right)$
: Let $\left({S', \circ'}\right)$ be an inverse completion of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$
: Let $\left({T', \circ'}\right)$ be an inverse completion of $\left({T, \circ}\right)$.
Then there is a unique isomorphism $\phi': S' \to T'$ extending $\phi$.
proof_text:
Let $C$ be the subsemigroup of cancellable elements of $S$.
It is proved that this is a semigroup by Cancellable Elements of Semigroup form Subsemigroup.
The set of cancellable elements of $T$ is $\phi \left({C}\right)$.
By the Extension Theorem for Homomorphisms, there is:
: A unique homomorphism $\phi'$ from $S'$ into $T'$ extending $\phi$
and:
: A unique homomorphism $\psi$ from $T'$ into $S'$ extending $\phi^{-1}$.
Therefore, $\psi \circ \phi'$ is an endomorphism of $S'$ whose restriction to $S$ is the inclusion mapping $\iota_S: S \to S'$:
$\forall x \in S: \iota \left({x}\right) = x$
From Inclusion Mapping is Monomorphism, $\iota_S$ is a monomorphism from $S$ into $S'$.
But by the Extension Theorem for Homomorphisms, the identity automorphism of $S'$ is the only endomorphism of $S'$ extending $\iota_S$ from $S$ into $S'$, so:
$\psi \circ \phi' = I_{S'}$
Similarly:
$\phi' \circ \psi = I_{T'}$
So by Bijection iff Left and Right Inverse, $\phi'$ is a bijection and therefore an isomorphism.
review_reason: Extending the map and its inverse gives composites extending the inclusions. Uniqueness of those extensions identifies both composites with identity maps.

title: Inverse Completion is Unique
theorem_text: An inverse completion of a commutative semigroup is unique up to isomorphism.
proof_text:
Let $T$ and $T'$ both be inverse completions of a commutative semigroup $S$ having cancellable elements.
Then from the Extension Theorem for Isomorphisms, there is a unique isomorphism $\phi: T \to T'$ satisfying $\forall x \in S: \phi \left({x}\right) = x$.
Hence the result.
review_reason: Extending the identity of S to its two inverse completions gives an isomorphism between them by the cited extension theorem.

title: Identity is only Idempotent Element in Group
theorem_text: Every group has exactly one idempotent element: the identity.
proof_text:
The Identity Element is Idempotent.
From the Cancellation Laws, all group elements are cancellable.
The result follows from Identity is only Idempotent Cancellable Element.
review_reason: The identity is idempotent and cancellation forces any idempotent g satisfying gg=g to equal the identity.

title: Power Set of Group under Induced Operation is Semigroup
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group.
Let $\struct {\powerset G, \circ_\mathcal P}$ be the algebraic structure consisting of the power set of $G$ and the operation induced on $\powerset G$ by $\circ$.
Then $\struct {\powerset G, \circ_\mathcal P}$ is a semigroup.
proof_text:
By definition a group is also a semigroup.
The result then follows from Power Set of Semigroup under Induced Operation is Semigroup.
review_reason: A group satisfies all semigroup axioms, so the stated power-set semigroup result specializes directly to G.

title: Inverse of Product of Subsets of Group
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group.
Let $X, Y \subseteq G$.
Then:
$\paren {X \circ Y}^{-1} = Y^{-1} \circ X^{-1}$
where $X^{-1}$ is the inverse of $X$.
proof_text:
Superset
We will show that $\forall z \in Y^{-1} \circ X^{-1}: z \in \left({X \circ Y}\right)^{-1}$, from which:
$Y^{-1} \circ X^{-1} \subseteq \left({X \circ Y}\right)^{-1}$
Let $z \in Y^{-1} \circ X^{-1}$.
By the definition of subset product:
$\exists x' \in X^{-1}, y' \in Y^{-1}: z = y' \circ x'$
Then by Inverse of Group Product:
$(2)\quad z^{-1} = x'^{-1} \circ y'^{-1}$
By the definition of inverse of subset:
$x'^{-1} \in X$ and $y'^{-1} \in Y$
By the definition of subset product:
$x'^{-1} \circ y'^{-1} \in X \circ Y$
Thus by $(2)$:
$z^{-1} \in X \circ Y$
By the definition of inverse of subset:
$z \in \left({X \circ Y}\right)^{-1}$
Subset
We will show that $\forall z \in \left({X \circ Y}\right)^{-1}: z \in Y^{-1} \circ X^{-1}$, from which:
$\left({X \circ Y}\right)^{-1} \subseteq Y^{-1} \circ X^{-1}$
Let $z \in \left({X \circ Y}\right)^{-1}$.
By the definition of inverse of subset:
$z^{-1} \in X \circ Y$
From Inverse of Inverse of Subset of Group:
$z^{-1} \in \left({ X^{-1} }\right)^{-1} \circ \left({ Y^{-1} }\right)^{-1}$
Thus by the superset proof above:
$z^{-1} \in \left({ Y^{-1} \circ X^{-1} }\right)^{-1}$
From the definition of inverse of subset:
$z \in Y^{-1} \circ X^{-1}$
review_reason: Taking inverses reverses the order of the two chosen factors, giving one inclusion. Applying that inclusion to the reversed inverse subsets and inverting again gives the other.

title: Regular Representations in Group are Permutations
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group.
Let $a \in G$ be any element of $G$.
Then the left regular representation $\lambda_a$ and the right regular representation $\rho_a$ are permutations of $G$.
proof_text:
This follows directly from the fact that all elements of a group are by definition invertible.
Therefore the result Regular Representation of Invertible Element is Permutation applies.
review_reason: Left and right translation by an invertible element are permutations by the cited result, and every element of a group is invertible.

title: Identity Mapping is Automorphism
theorem_text:
The identity mapping $I_S: \left({S, \circ}\right) \to \left({S, \circ}\right)$ on the algebraic structure $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is an automorphism.
Its image is $S$.
proof_text:
By definition, an automorphism is an isomorphism from an algebraic structure onto itself.
An isomorphism, in turn, is a bijective homomorphism.
From Identity Mapping is Bijection, the identity mapping $I_S: S \to S$ on the set $S$ is a bijection from $S$ onto itself.
Now we need to show it is a homomorphism.
Let $x, y \in S$. Then:
$$I_S \left({x \circ y}\right) = x \circ y$$
Definition of Identity Mapping
$$= I_S \left({x}\right) \circ I_S \left({y}\right)$$
Definition of Identity Mapping
Thus $I_S \left({x \circ y}\right) = I_S \left({x}\right) \circ I_S \left({y}\right)$ and the morphism property holds, proving that $I_S: S \to S$ is a homomorphism.
As $I_S$ is a bijection, its image is $S$.
review_reason: The identity map fixes both factors and their product and is a bijection onto S. These facts establish the automorphism and image claims.

title: Isomorphism of Abelian Groups
theorem_text:
Let $\phi: \struct {G, \circ} \to \struct {H, *}$ be a group isomorphism.
Then $\struct {G, \circ}$ is abelian if and only if $\struct {H, *}$ is abelian.
proof_text:
We have that Isomorphism Preserves Commutativity.
Thus:
$\forall x, y \in G: x \circ y = y \circ x \implies \map \phi x * \map \phi y = \map \phi y * \map \phi x$
Thus if $G$ is abelian, so is $H$.
As $\phi^{-1}: H \to G$ is also an isomorphism, it is clear that if $H$ is abelian, then so is $G$.
review_reason: Commutativity transfers through the isomorphism onto H and through its inverse onto G.

title: Symmetric Difference on Power Set forms Abelian Group
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a set such that $\O \subset S$ (that is, $S$ is non-empty).
Let $A * B$ be defined as the symmetric difference between $A$ and $B$.
Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$.
Then the algebraic structure $\struct {\powerset S, *}$ is an abelian group.
proof_text:
From Power Set is Closed under Symmetric Difference, we have that $\struct {\powerset S, *}$ is closed.
The result follows directly from Set System Closed under Symmetric Difference is Abelian Group.
review_reason: The power set is nonempty and closed under symmetric difference, meeting the cited abelian-group criterion for such a set system.

title: Group is Subgroup of Itself
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group.
Then:
$\struct {G, \circ} \le \struct {G, \circ}$
That is, a group is always a subgroup of itself.
proof_text:
By Set is Subset of Itself, we have that:
$G \subseteq G$
Thus $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a group which is a subset of $\struct {G, \circ}$, and therefore a subgroup of $\struct {G, \circ}$.
review_reason: Taking the underlying subset to be all of G gives the same group with exactly the inherited operation.

title: Identity of Subgroup
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$.
Let $H$ be a subgroup of group $G$.
Then the identity of $H$ is also $e$.
proof_text:
From the definition, a group is a monoid.
Also, all of its elements are cancellable.
The result then follows directly from the result for monoids each of whose elements are cancellable: Identity of Cancellable Monoid is Identity of Submonoid.
review_reason: The subgroup is a submonoid under the restricted operation and the ambient group is a cancellative monoid, so the cited shared-identity result applies.

title: Inverses in Subgroup
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a group.
Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.
Then for each $h \in H$, the inverse of $h$ in $H$ is the same as the inverse of $h$ in $G$.
proof_text:
Let $h \in H$.
Let:
$h'$ be the inverse of $h$ in $H$
$h^{-1}$ be the inverse of $h$ in $G$.
From Identity of Subgroup, $h \circ h' = e$.
From Inverse in Group is Unique, it follows that $h' = h^{-1}$.
review_reason: The product hh' equals the ambient identity because the subgroup shares that identity. Inverse uniqueness in G now identifies h' with the ambient inverse.

title: Elements of Group with Equal Images under Homomorphisms form Subgroup
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be groups.
Let $f: G \to H$ and $g: G \to H$ be group homomorphisms.
Then the set:
$S = \set {x \in G: \map f x = \map g x}$
is a subgroup of $G$.
proof_text:
Let the identities of $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be $e_G$ and $e_H$ respectively.
By Homomorphism to Group Preserves Identity:
$\map f {e_G} = \map g {e_G} = e_H$
Thus $e_G \in S$, and so $S \ne \O$.
Similarly, from Homomorphism to Group Preserves Inverses, $x \in S \implies x^{-1} \in S$.
Let $x, y \in S$. Then:
$$\map f {x \circ y} = \map f x * \map f y$$
Morphism Property
$$= \map g x * \map g y$$
Definition of $S$
$$= \map g {x \circ y}$$
Morphism Property
Thus $x \circ y \in S$.
So, by the Two-Step Subgroup Test:
$S \le G$
review_reason: Identity preservation gives a point of agreement. Product and inverse preservation make the agreement set closed under both operations, satisfying the subgroup test.

title: Group Homomorphism Preserves Subgroups
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {G_1, \circ}$ and $\struct {G_2, *}$ be groups.
Let $\phi: \struct {G_1, \circ} \to \struct {G_2, *}$ be a group homomorphism.
Then:
$H \le G_1 \implies \phi \sqbrk H \le G_2$
where:
$\phi \sqbrk H$ denotes the image of $H$ under $\phi$
$\le$ denotes subgroup.
That is, group homomorphism preserves subgroups.
proof_text:
Let $H \le G_1$.
First note that from Null Relation is Mapping iff Domain is Empty Set:
$H \ne \O \implies \phi \sqbrk H \ne \O$
and so $\phi \sqbrk H$ is not empty.
Next, let $x, y \in \phi \sqbrk H$.
Then:
$\exists h_1, h_2 \in H: x = \map \phi {h_1}, y = \map \phi {h_2}$
From the definition of Group Homomorphism, we have:
$\map \phi {h_1^{-1} \circ h_2} = x^{-1} * y$
Since $H$ is a subgroup:
$h_1^{-1} \circ h_2 \in H$
Hence:
$x^{-1} * y \in \phi \sqbrk H$
Thus from the One-Step Subgroup Test:
$\phi \sqbrk H \le G_2$
review_reason: The subgroup image is nonempty. Preimages h1 and h2 give a subgroup element h1-inverse times h2 mapping to the required target product.

title: Commutative Semigroup is Entropic Structure
theorem_text: A commutative semigroup is an entropic structure.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a commutative semigroup.
Let $a, b, c, d \in S$.
Then:
$$\paren {a \circ b} \circ \paren {c \circ d} = a \circ \paren {b \circ \paren {c \circ d} }$$
Associativity of $\circ$
$$= a \circ \paren {\paren {b \circ c} \circ d}$$
Associativity of $\circ$
$$= a \circ \paren {\paren {c \circ b} \circ d}$$
Commutativity of $\circ$
$$= a \circ \paren {c \circ \paren {b \circ d} }$$
Associativity of $\circ$
$$= \paren {a \circ c} \circ \paren {b \circ d}$$
Associativity of $\circ$
review_reason: Associativity removes the internal grouping, commutativity exchanges b and c, and associativity restores the grouping required by the entropic identity.

title: Ring is not Empty
theorem_text: A ring cannot be empty.
proof_text:
In a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$, $\struct {R, +}$ forms a group.
From Group is not Empty, the group $\struct {R, +}$ contains at least the identity, so cannot be empty.
So every ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ contains at least the identity for ring addition.
review_reason: The additive group supplies a zero element belonging to the ring, ruling out the empty set.

title: Unity of Ring is Unique
theorem_text: A ring can have no more than one unity.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring.
If $\struct {R, \circ}$ has an identity, then it is a monoid.
From Identity of Monoid is Unique, it follows that such an identity is unique.
review_reason: Under associative ring multiplication, the existence of a unity gives a monoid, which has a unique identity.

title: GCD for Negative Integers
theorem_text:
$\gcd \set {a, b} = \gcd \set {\size a, b} = \gcd \set {a, \size b} = \gcd \set {\size a, \size b}$
Alternatively, this can be put:
$\gcd \set {a, b} = \gcd \set {-a, b} = \gcd \set {a, -b} = \gcd \set {-a, -b}$
which follows directly from the above.
proof_text:
Note that $\size a = \pm a$.
Suppose that:
$u \divides a$
where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.
Then:
$\exists q \in \Z: a = q u$
Then:
$\size a = \pm q u = \paren {\pm q} u \implies u \divides \size a$
So every divisor of $a$ is a divisor of $\size a$.
Similarly, note that:
$a = \pm \size a$
so every divisor of $\size a$ is a divisor of $a$.
So it follows that the common divisors of $a$ and $b$ are the same as those of $a$ and $\size b$, and so on.
In particular:
$\gcd \set {a, b} = \gcd \set {a, \size b}$
and so on.
review_reason: Negating an integer negates its quotient by a given divisor. Thus replacing either argument by its absolute value preserves the entire common-divisor set.
